summary:
Chocó is a department of Colombia on the Pacific coast, standing under the national framework of Colombia. No Chocó-specific legal provision, enforcement practice, or documented incident against a trans person was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment carried by the parent record applies.

What bears on Chocó is the territorial violence and displacement inflicted by armed actors. Reporting on Colombia's armed groups frames being queer in parts of the country as signing one's own death sentence, and killings continued at the hands of armed gangs even after the Millerey video shocked the country. In Caquetá, armed groups distributed flyers and WhatsApp messages naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was given one week by three armed men to leave town, hid, then fled at night, and a second trans woman reported a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, with discrimination limiting trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. The source inventory identifies trans women as being displaced from departments such as Chocó, where armed groups rather than departmental police regulate conduct.

The national framework the visitor stands under includes protection as victims of armed conflict, the element of that framework relevant to Chocó, alongside a national LGBTI policy covering rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a bar on national entities refusing to recognise same-sex couples.
tangentialFactors:
Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Colombia since 1981, the right to change legal gender has been recognised since 1993, a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016 making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so, and same-sex couples gained joint adoption rights in 2015. These are national provisions carried by the parent record and are noted here only as the framework within which Chocó sits.

The Caquetá campaign is a departmental example of the pattern of armed-group 'social cleansing' that also affects Chocó; it is not a Chocó finding. Raw national killing counts (eight trans women killed February to April 2024, 41 in 2023) are national figures and do not measure risk in Chocó specifically.
localsOnly: Residents of Chocó live under a security environment in which armed groups rather than departmental police regulate conduct, and trans women are reported as being displaced from the department. The national policy text covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict applies to residents, as does protection as victims of armed conflict.
outOfScopeNotes: No Chocó-specific legal provision, enforcement practice, or documented incident against a trans person was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment carried by the parent record applies. Whether Chocó's own departmental administration has issued any LGBTI-specific measure, and whether any trans person has been killed or displaced within Chocó specifically, remain unresolved and not sourced here. The Caquetá flyer campaign and displacement of trans women 'from departments such as Chocó' are reported at the national or other-department level and are not documented as occurring inside Chocó.
